opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it comes down to two things: what the technology can reliably do today, and where the value is clear enough that someone will pay for it.

The home is the hardest environment you can imagine for a robot. Every house is different. There's clutter, pets, kids, stairs, carpets, things moved since yesterday. And the tasks people want help with, like folding laundry, loading the dishwasher, or tidying up, need really dexterous manipulation and a lot of common sense. There's also very little tolerance for failure. If a robot breaks a glass or bumps into a child, that's a big problem. On top of that, the price has to be in consumer territory, comparable to a car or less, which is very hard with today's hardware costs. I think home robots will come, but it's a longer road.

Industrial settings are much more structured. You have defined workflows, trained staff, safety procedures, and often a very clear problem: inspection rounds in a plant, moving material between stations, or working in places that are dangerous or unpleasant for people. The environment still has plenty of variability, which is exactly where learning-based approaches like reinforcement learning in simulation help. But it's bounded variability, and you can actually validate performance against it.

The economics also make sense. A company can compare the robot to labor costs, downtime, or safety incidents and calculate a return. They can afford a more expensive machine if it runs multiple shifts. And because they're operating fleets, you get data from real deployments, which lets you improve the system much faster.

So for us, industry isn't the smaller ambition. It's the path that lets us ship real products now, learn from real-world operation, and mature the hardware and the AI. Many of the capabilities we build there, like robust locomotion, navigation, and eventually manipulation, are the same foundations you'll eventually need in the home.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts structured industrial environments with varied homes, but it does not explain that sending an engineer to prepare each warehouse deployment is practical while providing equivalent onsite setup for every household is not.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the home is actually the hardest environment you can possibly pick. People look at a kitchen or a living room and think, well, that's a very simple place for a robot, but it's the opposite. Every home is different, the objects are different, they're in different places every day, there are kids and pets, and the tolerance for failure is essentially zero. If the robot drops a glass or bumps into someone's grandmother, that's a very bad day, and there's nobody there to help the robot recover. So you need a level of generalization and safety that, honestly, I don't think the technology is at yet, even though the demos look great.

Industrial settings are almost the inverse of that. The environment is structured, or at least semi-structured. You know roughly what the tasks are, you can constrain the problem, and there's a safety culture already in place. People are used to working around machines, there are protocols, there are people on site who can intervene if something goes wrong. So you can deploy something that's imperfect and still be useful, and then you learn from it.

The second part is really the economics. In a factory or a warehouse or a logistics setting, the value of the robot is very easy to quantify. There's a task that's dangerous, or repetitive, or there's a labor shortage, and you can put a number on it. That means a customer can justify paying what the hardware actually costs today. In the home, people expect something at the price of an appliance, and we're nowhere near that with legged robots or humanoids. So you'd be building a product that's technically very hard and also commercially very hard at the same time.

And from my perspective, coming from the research side, I actually care about the home problem a lot. I think it's where the most interesting questions are. But the way you get there is by getting robots out into the real world at scale, collecting data, finding all the failure modes you never see in the lab. Industry is where you can do that today while having a business that makes sense. So I see it less as giving up on homes and more as the path that actually leads there.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts industrial sites with homes and mentions onsite staff who can intervene, but it does not explain that sending an engineer to prepare each warehouse deployment is practical while providing equivalent setup for every household is not.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how well you can define the problem. In an industrial setting, you can identify a specific task, understand the environment, and measure whether the robot is actually useful. How much time does it save? How reliably can it do the job? That gives you a concrete target to build toward.

In somebody’s home, there’s much more variation. Every home is different, things move around, and people expect a robot to handle a whole range of tasks. Even defining what successful deployment looks like becomes harder.

So it’s not that homes aren’t interesting. But for a robotics company, an industrial application gives you a more manageable starting point: solve a valuable problem in a relatively structured environment, get the system working reliably, and expand from there.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts structured industrial tasks with variable homes, but does not mention sending an engineer to prepare a warehouse deployment or why equivalent onsite setup for every household is impractical.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, it comes down to having a well-defined problem and a clear reason for someone to pay for the solution. In an industrial setting, you can identify a particular task, understand how often it needs to be done, and measure the value of automating it. You also have more control over the environment, so you can narrow the problem enough to build something reliable.

In a home, the expectations are much broader. Every home is different, there are all kinds of objects and situations, and people want a robot that can do lots of things without much setup. You have to solve a much more general problem, while keeping the price low enough that someone would actually buy it.

That doesn’t mean home robotics won’t happen. But industrial applications give us a practical starting point where we can deliver value with a more focused capability, learn from deployment, and expand from there.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts controlled industrial environments with varied homes and mentions that home robots need little setup, but it does not explain that sending an engineer to prepare a warehouse deployment is practical while providing equivalent onsite setup for every household is not.
